title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
hook: a teaching book tells its reader that all the reading won't settle them until they forget it all

segments.voice: Yesterday, shukti and the sage's test: why does the king still reach for silver that's only a shell? Silver, or a shell?

Somewhere on a shelf there's a stack of books about letting go, and every one of them is something else to hold on to. The Ashtavakra Gita seems to know that joke. Deep in the book, the sage says something that could make a diligent reader put the page down. You can talk about the scriptures and listen to them, my child, as much as you like. But you won't rest in yourself until you forget it all. A book telling its reader that the reading isn't the point. And a few verses later, it praises a master of idleness.
screen: `BOOKS ABOUT LETTING GO.` → `FORGET IT ALL.` → `A MASTER OF IDLENESS.`

segments.voice: This is chapter sixteen, in paraphrase. After the line about forgetting, the sage goes on. You may enjoy, you may work, you may meditate, but the mind will still long for what lies beyond all that, where wanting goes quiet. Then something like a diagnosis: everyone is unhappy because of their striving, and nobody notices. Then a verse that can sound like a joke. Happy is the great idler, the one for whom even opening and closing the eyes is a bother. No one else. Read straight, that's a blessing on the couch. The verses around it point another way. Each is about one kind of effort: the strain of the one who thinks I am the doer, the black snake from a few days ago. The great idler isn't someone who won't wash the dishes. It's someone in whom that inner straining has stopped. The dishes may still get washed; nobody inside is clenching about it. Teachers often read the forgetting the same way. The sage isn't asking Janaka to forget his kindness or his duties. He's asking him to stop holding the teaching like a possession, a set of correct ideas to defend. Knowledge carried like luggage is still something extra to carry. Here the book turns on itself, gently: it has spent pages pointing at freedom, and now the pointing has to drop away too. The Vivekachudamani gave a warning like it, about clever talk of scripture, and the Ashtavakra Gita gives it in its own way.
screen: `FORGET IT ALL.` · `UNHAPPY BECAUSE OF STRIVING.` · `THE GREAT IDLER: NO INNER STRAINING.` · `DON'T CARRY THE TEACHING LIKE LUGGAGE.` · then, large: `THE POINTING DROPS AWAY TOO.`

segments.voice: For these minutes, try the sage's kind of idleness: don't manage the breath, don't follow a technique, don't try to remember anything from this week, not even today's lesson. If you catch yourself trying to sit well, let that go too. Whatever is here, let it be here, eyes open or closed, as they like.
Great idler, the one in whom the inner striving has stopped, happy because there's no more clenching inside. Today, the Ashtavakra Gita's hardest line: forget it all.
Your line: forget it all. Even the teaching can be set down. Day one thousand three, done.

howItsDone: Some teachers of the Ashtavakra Gita explain its praise of idleness as the end of inner striving rather than of outward work, and its call to forget everything as letting go of holding the teaching itself as a possession.

chat.says: So the book says the happiest person is the laziest one?
options: No, it means the inner straining stops; the dishes may still get washed.
Yes, it says stop working and let other people take care of everything.
Yes, it says skip your duties, since nothing you do matters anyway.
chat.meaning: The great idler in chapter sixteen isn't someone who won't work. It's someone in whom the clenching of I am the doer has stopped.
